title: A flux-mean bound shows that slow edges can hide century-long dust dimming from a PS1-Gaia epoch test
abstract: We test the scope of an onset-rate limit for slow dust dimming of field dwarfs. We prove that the difference between two positive flux-mean magnitudes is at most the maximum light-curve slope times the largest separation in an optimal pairing of their epoch distributions. For times inside the published PS1 and Gaia intervals, any sampling misses a noiseless 0.5-mag trapezoid with 15-percent-duration edges if its duration exceeds 82.22 years at a 0.3-mag threshold. Exact integrals for uniform epochs give a zero window at the tested duration of 50 years, while fixed 1.2-year edges keep a 6.616-year window through 500 years. Synthetic asynchronous colour cuts have little effect on tested smooth events. Thus the reported eight-year rate limit cannot bound all slow events without an edge-time distribution. This is a proof and synthetic selection study, not a revised measured rate, new object or estimate of a hidden population. Real pipeline weights, noise, catalogue cuts and vetting require separate injection tests. Code, checks, model outputs and source hashes are included.

display.caption: Exact model control times for fixed and duration-scaled edges, with synthetic multiband cadence checks. These curves do not measure real survey completeness.
